solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Cuckoo grips twig

indicators.note: cuckoo is slang for crazy, and letters that have gone crazy scramble themselves

explanation.surface: A cuckoo clutches a twig in its claws.
explanation.walkthrough: Cuckoo looks like the bird doing the gripping, but here it is the adjective meaning crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a small shoot snapped from a plant, like a sprig of parsley, is a little twig.

clue.text: Splinter group determined to welcome Conservative

indicators.note: a host who welcomes a guest takes them inside, so SET takes in C

explanation.surface: A breakaway faction is resolved to take in a Tory member.
explanation.walkthrough: C for Conservative is the usual abbreviation for the British Tory party, which fits the political surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a sect is a group that has broken away from a larger religious or political body.

clue.text: Raised berth space

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising a word lifts its bottom letter to the top, so it reads upward

blocks.note: to moor a boat is to berth it

explanation.surface: A bunk bed set high up to free some floor space.
explanation.walkthrough: Berth looks like a noun (a bed on a ship or train), but it is the verb for tying up a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of room to move or no room left: available space.

clue.text: With aim to grasp information technology, I work solo

indicators.note: to grasp something is to hold it in your hand, so GOAL closes around IT

blocks.note: IT is the usual short form
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone keen to master computing decides to learn it without help.
explanation.walkthrough: The I looks like the subject of 'work solo', but it belongs to the wordplay as ONE.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: to go it alone is to do something by yourself, without help or partners.

clue.text: Puzzled finding flightless birds in garden plot

indicators.note: the birds are placed in the plot, so their letters sit inside BED

blocks.note: emus are large Australian birds that cannot fly

explanation.surface: A gardener is baffled to discover ostrich-like birds among the vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: Garden plot is a crossword favourite for BED; plot alone could suggest a storyline.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone bemused is bewildered and cannot make sense of what is happening.

clue.text: Book dragged leaving learner irritated

indicators.note: something leaving a word walks out of it, so L departs from LUGGED

blocks.note: B is the standard abbreviation for book
L for learner, as on British L-plates

explanation.surface: A reader was annoyed at having to haul a heavy book around.
explanation.walkthrough: L for learner comes from the L-plates new drivers display in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal synonym: something that bugs you gets on your nerves, so bugged means annoyed.

clue.text: Infuriated when barrier gets erected

indicators.note: erecting something stands it upright, so in a down clue the word reads from the bottom up

blocks.note: a dam is a barrier across a river

explanation.surface: Someone is furious that a fence has gone up next door.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a neighbour's fence; the barrier needed is one across a river.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal sense: mad in everyday speech often means angry rather than insane.

clue.text: Horse half ignored by stalking cat

indicators.note: ignoring half of a word leaves the other half, so STALKING keeps STAL

blocks.note: a lion is a big cat

explanation.surface: A horse goes half-unnoticed by a big cat hunting it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stalking cat' reads as a lion on the hunt; the two words give separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a stallion is a particular kind of horse, the uncastrated male.

clue.text: Use symptoms to identify disorder in sea dog

indicators.note: letters in disorder are out of order, so IN SEA DOG is jumbled

explanation.surface: A ship's doctor works out what illness an old sailor has.
explanation.walkthrough: Disorder poses as the illness to be identified, but it is the instruction to rearrange; a sea dog is an old sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: doctors diagnose by reading symptoms and naming the condition behind them.

clue.text: Celtic ultimately not winning final

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so take the end letter of Celtic

explanation.surface: Celtic end up beaten in a cup final.
explanation.walkthrough: Celtic is a Glasgow football club, which makes 'final' look like a match rather than an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: closing remarks or the closing stages are the final ones.

clue.text: Regularly seen admiral near woman

indicators.note: something seen regularly turns up at even intervals, so take every other letter

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: An admiral is often spotted with a lady by his side.
explanation.walkthrough: Crosswords often define a first name just as 'woman' or 'girl'.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Diana is one of many women's names, so any woman could be one.

clue.text: Fruit transported to new realm

indicators.note: transported things are moved to new positions, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Produce is shipped off to a far-off land.
explanation.walkthrough: Transported sounds like shipping the fruit, but it is the instruction to rearrange the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the watermelon is one kind of fruit.

clue.text: Coat guy wrapped around poorly prime minister

indicators.note: wrapping something around goes outside it, so MAN encloses ILL

explanation.surface: A man wraps his coat around a leader who is feeling unwell.
explanation.walkthrough: Harold Macmillan was British prime minister from 1957 to 1963; mac is British for a raincoat.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Harold Macmillan is one of the UK's past prime ministers.

clue.text: Likely for newborn to consume liquids primarily

indicators.note: whatever you consume goes inside you, so BABE takes L in
primarily means first of all, so take the first letter of liquids

explanation.surface: A new baby will probably take mostly fluids.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Likely for newborn' reads as one phrase, but for is PRO and likely stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: what is probable is likely to happen or be true.

clue.text: Simplicity of some ideas, in essence

indicators.note: some of the following words means only part of their letters, taken in a run

explanation.surface: Good ideas are, at heart, simple.
explanation.walkthrough: In essence sounds like a summary, but its letters carry the end of the answer; the comma is ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the easiness of a task is its simplicity.

clue.text: I’m unsure backing a relative’s cause

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so ER is written in reverse

blocks.note: er is the noise of someone hesitating

explanation.surface: Someone hesitates over supporting a family member's campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: Backing looks like support for the cause, and the ’s stands for 'is', joining wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the reason for something is its cause.

clue.text: With sides leaving, game with netted sticks is over

indicators.note: a word's sides are its two ends, so they depart from LACROSSE

blocks.note: lacrosse is played with sticks that have a net at the end

explanation.surface: The teams walk off and the lacrosse match is finished.
explanation.walkthrough: Over reads as 'finished', but it is the definition in the sense of from one side to the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in one sense: to walk over the bridge is to walk across it.

clue.text: Threaten mischievous sprite with death

blocks.note: an imp is a small mischievous spirit

explanation.surface: An impish creature menaces someone with killing.
explanation.walkthrough: Threaten here is intransitive, as danger threatens or looms, not as one person threatens another.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something impending hangs over you, about to happen, just as a storm threatens.

clue.text: Wedding helper’s offer to accommodate trips with mother

indicators.note: to accommodate guests is to take them in, so BID houses RIDES and MA

explanation.surface: A wedding helper offers to put up a mother on her travels.
explanation.walkthrough: The ’s stands for 'is', linking the definition to the wordplay rather than marking possession.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a bridesmaid attends the bride and helps her on the wedding day.

clue.text: Revolution advanced to north state

indicators.note: north is up on a map, so in a down clue the letters read upward

blocks.note: rev is short for a revolution of an engine
A is the abbreviation for advanced, as in A-level

explanation.surface: An uprising pushes on towards a northern state.
explanation.walkthrough: State looks like a country's region, but it is the verb meaning declare; revolution is the engine sense, not an uprising.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym of the verb: to aver is to state something as fact.

clue.text: Begrudge emissary forgetting nothing

indicators.note: what you forget goes missing, so the O drops out of ENVOY

explanation.surface: Someone resents a diplomat who has achieved nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing is O, the zero-shaped letter, a common crossword swap.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to envy or begrudge someone is to resent their good fortune.

clue.text: Sound from animal left in pound

indicators.note: what is left in the pound is inside it, so L sits within BEAT

explanation.surface: Noise from a creature abandoned in the animal pound.
explanation.walkthrough: Pound looks like an animal shelter, but it is the verb meaning beat.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a bleat is the cry a sheep or goat makes.

clue.text: Hill degenerate climbs

indicators.note: a climber goes up, so in a down clue the word reads from the bottom

blocks.note: to rot is to decay, degenerate

explanation.surface: A disreputable person scrambles up a hillside.
explanation.walkthrough: Degenerate reads as a noun for a bad person; it is the verb. Tors are the rocky hilltops of places like Dartmoor in England.
explanation.definitionFit: A regional word: in south-west England a tor is a rocky hill.

clue.text: Rouse characters held back by an evil nemesis

indicators.note: characters are letters, and these ones are held within the words that follow
back means the letters are read in reverse

explanation.surface: A hero is stirred into action but held back by a wicked arch-enemy.
explanation.walkthrough: Characters looks like people in a story, but it means letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to enliven a party is to rouse it, giving it more life.

clue.text: Made certain knight reused battered shields

indicators.note: something battered is knocked out of shape, so REUSED is rearranged
a shield covers what it protects, so the jumbled letters go around N

blocks.note: N for knight, as in chess notation

explanation.surface: A knight checked that his recycled, dented shields would do.
explanation.walkthrough: Shields looks like a knight's kit, but it is the verb for going around N.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to ensure something is to make certain it happens.

clue.text: Residing in New York, concerned with turning very anxious

indicators.note: a resident lives inside a place, so the letters sit inside NY
turning round reverses direction, so RE becomes ER

explanation.surface: A New York resident preoccupied with change is very jittery.
explanation.walkthrough: Very looks like it intensifies anxious, but it is just the letter V.
explanation.definitionFit: A British sense: nervy means jumpy or anxious, though in America it can mean cheeky.
